title: Purposes, uses, advantages and disadvantages of statistical representations
summary: Choose a representation from the data structure, comparison task and audience, and justify the choice using specific strengths and limitations.
objectives: Match tables, bar graphs, pictograms, line graphs and pie charts to their main purposes.
Explain a representation’s advantages and disadvantages in the context of a task.
Recommend a clear display from the data structure and the reader’s needs.

blocks.text: A representation is useful when it makes the intended comparison accurate and efficient. First identify whether the data consist of separate categories, ordered measurements, change over time or parts of one total. Then identify what the reader must do: look up exact values, compare groups, follow change or judge composition.

The table below gives strong default choices. A table serves exact lookup, a bar graph makes category lengths easy to compare, a pictogram presents a few categories to a general audience, a line graph follows ordered change, and a pie chart highlights a small number of parts within one meaningful whole. These are guidelines rather than automatic rules; the audience and amount of data also matter.

sections.title: Name both the strength and the limitation

blocks.text: Tables preserve exact values and can handle many entries, but patterns may be slow to notice. Bar graphs make differences between categories visible, but crowded labels or too many categories reduce clarity. Pictograms can be engaging for a small audience, but partial symbols and decorative pictures can make precise comparison difficult.

Line graphs reveal direction, turning points and rate of change across an ordered variable, but connecting points may imply values between observations. Pie charts communicate a few shares of one whole, but similar angles are hard to compare and many small sectors become unreadable. A reasoned recommendation should link one of these properties to the stated task.

sections.title: Worked example: exact lookup or category comparison

prompt.text: A community programme records participant counts for 12 activities. Coordinators need exact counts for room bookings, while a presentation should show which activities are most popular. Recommend a representation for each purpose.

content.text: For room bookings, the reader must retrieve many exact values. Use a labelled table because every activity and count can be read directly without estimating a bar length.
For the presentation, the main task is rapid comparison across separate activities. Use a bar graph with a zero baseline and a common scale.
If space is limited, sort the bars consistently or show only a clearly stated subset. Do not replace missing categories with an unexplained ‘other’ group.

sections.verification_note: The recommendations change because the tasks change, even though the underlying data are identical: the table preserves exact counts and the bar graph makes relative category sizes visible.

sections.title: Worked example: compare two time series

prompt.text: Monthly rainfall for two towns is recorded for one year. The reader must compare seasonal patterns and identify months when the towns move differently. Choose and design a suitable display.

content.text: Months form an ordered time variable, and the task concerns patterns of change. Choose a double line graph, one line for each town.

Use the same vertical scale for both series, plot the months at equal horizontal intervals and include a clear legend. Distinct line styles should remain understandable without relying only on colour.

A grouped bar graph could compare individual months, but 24 bars would make the year-long pattern harder to follow. A pie chart is unsuitable because monthly rainfall is not being presented as shares of one fixed total.

sections.verification_note: The chosen graph matches the ordered structure, permits month-by-month comparison on one scale and makes rises, falls and crossings between the two series visible.

blocks.text: A correct graph still needs a descriptive title, units, readable labels, a sensible scale and a legend when several series appear. Use consistent visual encodings: equal quantities should have equal lengths, areas or angles. Avoid three-dimensional decoration that changes apparent size without adding information.

Consider accessibility and the likely reading setting. Patterns or labels can distinguish series that colour alone would hide. A brief source note, sample size and time period help readers judge whether the display supports a broad conclusion. When no single representation serves every purpose, a concise graph can be paired with a small table of exact values.

prompt.text: Use code 1 for table, 2 for bar graph, 3 for pictogram, 4 for line graph and 5 for pie chart. Which code best shows a temperature trend measured each hour?

feedback.text: Hourly observations are ordered in time and the task is to follow change, so a line graph is the strongest default choice: code 4.

blocks.text: Identify the data structure and the reader’s task before choosing a display. Do not choose a graph because it looks decorative.
Justify the choice with a relevant advantage, then acknowledge a limitation that matters in the same context.
Use clear titles, labels, units, scales and legends. Pair a graph with a table when readers need both a visual pattern and exact lookup.
